title: RF Amplifier Design
description: Design single-stage transistor amplifiers from S-parameters: power gains, stability tests, unilateral and conjugate matching, and the noise–gain trade-off.

study.title: The transistor as a two-port
study.body: At RF a transistor (with its bias) is characterized by measured S-parameters at each frequency. Typical values: $|S_{21}|$ = 2–5 (gain), $|S_{12}|$ = 0.02–0.1 (a little feedback), $|S_{11}|$ and $|S_{22}|$ = 0.3–0.8. The amplifier is the transistor between an input matching network (presenting $\Gamma_S$) and an output matching network (presenting $\Gamma_L$). Because $S_{12} \neq 0$, what one port sees depends on the termination of the other.

study.title: Three power gains
study.body: **Transducer gain** $G_T = P_L/P_{avs}$: power delivered to the load per power available from the source; this is what the system sees. **Operating gain** $G = P_L/P_{in}$ ignores input mismatch; **available gain** $G_A = P_{avn}/P_{avs}$ assumes a conjugately matched load. All three are equal when both ports are conjugately matched. With $\Gamma_S = \Gamma_L = 0$ (50 Ω on both sides), $G_T = |S_{21}|^2$.

study.title: Unilateral design
study.body: If $S_{12}$ is small, set it to zero: then $\Gamma_{in} = S_{11}$ and $\Gamma_{out} = S_{22}$, and the transducer gain splits into three factors: input match, transistor, output match. Each match factor is largest for a conjugate match, $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ and $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$. In dB the three gains simply add.
study.formula: \begin{aligned}& G_{TU} = G_S\,G_0\,G_L,\quad G_0 = |S_{21}|^2\\ & G_S = \frac{1-|\Gamma_S|^2}{|1 - S_{11}\Gamma_S|^2}\\ & G_{S,max} = \frac{1}{1-|S_{11}|^2}\ \text{at}\ \Gamma_S = S_{11}^*\end{aligned}

study.title: Stability
study.body: If some passive load makes $|\Gamma_{in}| > 1$ (or some source makes $|\Gamma_{out}| > 1$), the port has a negative resistance and the amplifier can oscillate. A two-port is **unconditionally stable** at a frequency if no passive termination can do this. Rollett's test needs two conditions; the μ test needs one. Check every frequency where the transistor has gain, not only the design frequency. A potentially unstable transistor can be stabilized with a small series or shunt resistor at a port, at the cost of gain and noise.

study.title: Maximum gain: conjugate matching
study.body: With $S_{12} \neq 0$ the best design matches both ports at once ($\Gamma_S = \Gamma_{in}^*$, $\Gamma_L = \Gamma_{out}^*$), which is only possible for an unconditionally stable device. The resulting maximum available gain depends only on K and the forward/reverse ratio. For K < 1 the useful figure is the **maximum stable gain** (the same with K = 1). The unilateral figure of merit U bounds the error of the unilateral conjugate design ($\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$, $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$).

study.title: Worked example
study.body:
A FET at 4 GHz: $S_{11}$ = 0.65∠−140°, $S_{21}$ = 3.2∠75°, $S_{12}$ = 0.06∠50°, $S_{22}$ = 0.45∠−50°.
- Δ = 0.207∠−149°, K = 1.09: unconditionally stable (μ = 1.05)
- $G_0$ = 20 log 3.2 = 10.1 dB, $G_{S,max}$ = 2.4 dB, $G_{L,max}$ = 1.0 dB: $G_{TU,max}$ = 13.5 dB
- U = 0.122: the unilateral design's real gain lies within −1.0 … +1.1 dB of 13.5 dB
- Simultaneous conjugate match: $G_{T,max}$ = 53.3 × (1.09 − 0.43) = 15.5 dB (MSG = 17.3 dB)
- Unilateral matches: $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ = 0.65∠+140°, $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$ = 0.45∠+50°

study.title: Low noise versus gain
study.body: A transistor has its lowest noise figure $F_{min}$ for one source reflection $\Gamma_{opt}$, which is generally **not** $S_{11}^*$. Away from it the noise rises at a rate set by the noise resistance $R_N$. An LNA's input is therefore matched for noise, not gain: it gives up some gain and accepts an input mismatch. Circles of constant F and constant $G_S$ on the Smith chart show the trade-off; balanced amplifiers or isolators can restore the input match.

steps.title: What each port sees
steps.body: The input matching network presents $\Gamma_S$ to the transistor, the output network $\Gamma_L$. The small reverse transmission $S_{12}$ couples the ports: the output reflection depends on the source termination and vice versa.

steps.title: Which gain?
steps.body: Transducer gain $G_T$ compares the load power with the power the source could deliver: it includes every mismatch and is what you measure in a 50 Ω system. Operating gain G uses the power actually entering the amplifier; available gain $G_A$ the power the amplifier could deliver to a matched load.

steps.prompt: Match each gain to its definition.
pairs: Power available at the output / power available from the source
steps.explanation: $G_T$ includes both mismatches; $G$ ignores the input mismatch (it starts from the power that actually enters); $G_A$ ignores the output mismatch (it assumes a conjugate load). With $\Gamma_S = \Gamma_L = 0$ the transducer gain reduces to $|S_{21}|^2$.

steps.prompt: A unilateral transistor ($S_{12}$ ≈ 0) has $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°, $|S_{21}|$ = {{m21}}, $S_{22}$ = {{m22}}∠{{a22}}°. The matching networks present $\Gamma_S$ = {{GS}} and $\Gamma_L$ = {{GL}}. Find the transducer gain in dB.
When a transistor is placed directly between a 50 Ω source and a 50 Ω load, its transducer gain is $|S_{21}|^2$.
steps.explanation: True. With $\Gamma_S = \Gamma_L = 0$ every factor in the $G_T$ formula except $|S_{21}|^2$ becomes 1. That is exactly how $S_{21}$ is defined: forward transmission between matched (50 Ω) terminations.

steps.title: Maximum unilateral gain
steps.body: For a unilateral transistor the input and output can be matched separately. A conjugate match ($\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$, $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$) gives the largest $G_S$ and $G_L$. A badly matched transistor gains the most from matching.

ask.prompt: How much gain (dB) does the conjugate input match add?
What is the maximum unilateral transducer gain in dB?

steps.prompt: A unilateral transistor has $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°. Which source reflection coefficient gives the maximum gain?
steps.explanation: Maximum $G_S$ needs a conjugate match: $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ = **{{m11}}∠{{-a11}}°** (same magnitude, opposite angle). $\Gamma_S = S_{11}$ forgets the conjugate and gives less gain; a magnitude above 1 is not passive.

steps.title: Negative resistance
steps.body: Feedback through $S_{12}$ can make $|\Gamma_{in}| > 1$ for some loads: the input then has a negative resistance and, with the right source, the amplifier oscillates. Rollett's test: the two-port is unconditionally stable if K > 1 **and** |Δ| < 1.

steps.prompt: A transistor has $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°, $S_{21}$ = {{m21}}∠{{a21}}°, $S_{12}$ = {{m12}}∠{{a12}}°, $S_{22}$ = {{m22}}∠{{a22}}°, giving K = {{K}} and |Δ| = {{sqrt(D2)}}. It is unconditionally stable at this frequency.
steps.explanation: Rollett: unconditionally stable if K > 1 **and** |Δ| < 1. Here K = {{K}} and |Δ| = {{sqrt(D2)}}, so check K − 1 = {{K-1}} and 1 − |Δ| = {{1-sqrt(D2)}}: the transistor is unconditionally stable only if both are positive. If K < 1, some passive source or load inside the Smith chart makes a port reflection exceed 1: potentially unstable.

steps.title: One-number test and cures
steps.body: Edwards and Sinsky's μ is a single test: μ > 1 means unconditionally stable, and a larger μ means more margin. A potentially unstable transistor can still be used if the chosen $\Gamma_S$ and $\Gamma_L$ stay in the stable regions (outside the stability circles), or it is stabilized with a small resistor at the input or output.

steps.explanation: Δ = {{Dr}} + j({{Di}}). $\Delta S_{11}^*$ = {{Dr*c11+Di*s11}} + j({{Di*c11-Dr*s11}}), so $S_{22} - \Delta S_{11}^*$ = {{er}} + j({{ei}}) with magnitude {{sqrt(er^2+ei^2)}}. μ = (1 − {{m11^2}}) / ({{sqrt(er^2+ei^2)}} + {{m12*m21}}) = **{{mu}}**: μ > 1 means unconditionally stable.

steps.prompt: Your transistor has K = 0.8 at the design frequency. Which is a standard way to make a stable amplifier with it?
options: Add a small series or shunt resistor at the input or output (resistive loading)
Conjugately match both ports: that always makes the amplifier stable
Raise the gain with a larger output matching inductor
Nothing: K < 1 only matters for power amplifiers
steps.explanation: Resistive loading adds loss exactly where the negative resistance would appear, raising K above 1 at the cost of some gain (and noise, if at the input). A simultaneous conjugate match does not even exist for K < 1. Alternatively, choose $\Gamma_S$ and $\Gamma_L$ well inside the stable regions.

steps.prompt: Match each statement to what it means.
steps.explanation: Rollett needs two conditions, μ only one. A reflection coefficient larger than 1 means the port returns more power than it receives: a negative resistance. The stability circles on the Smith chart separate the safe terminations from the dangerous ones.

steps.prompt: Find the maximum unilateral transducer gain (dB) of a transistor with $|S_{11}|$ = {{m11}}, $|S_{21}|$ = {{m21}}, $|S_{22}|$ = {{m22}}.
A unilateral transistor has $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°. The input network presents $\Gamma_S$ = {{mS}}∠{{aS}}°. Find the input matching gain $G_S$ in dB.
A transistor has $|S_{11}|$ = {{m11}}, $|S_{21}|$ = {{m21}}, $|S_{12}|$ = {{m12}}, $|S_{22}|$ = {{m22}}. You design it as if it were unilateral, with $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ and $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$.

ask.prompt: Find the unilateral figure of merit U.
By at most how many dB can the real gain exceed the unilateral prediction?
ask.explanation: U = {{U}}. The upper bound is $1/(1-U)^2$: −20 log(1 − {{U}}) = **{{-20*log10(1-U)}} dB** (the lower bound is −20 log(1 + U) = {{-20*log10(1+U)}} dB). A few tenths of a dB justifies the unilateral assumption.

ask.prompt: Both ports are conjugately matched at the same time. Find the maximum transducer gain in dB.
Find its maximum stable gain MSG (the value $G_{T,max}$ would reach for K → 1) in dB.

steps.prompt: $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}° (blue). The input network presents $\Gamma_S$ (red) with $|\Gamma_S|$ = {{m11}}. Drag its angle to maximize the input matching gain $G_S$.
steps.explanation: $G_S$ is largest for the conjugate match $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$: the mirror image of $S_{11}$ in the real axis, angle **{{-a11}}°**. Then $G_S = 1/(1-|S_{11}|^2)$ = {{-10*log10(1-m11^2)}} dB. The lowest $G_S$ on this circle lies diametrically opposite, at $\Gamma_S = -S_{11}^*$ (angle {{mod(-a11, 360)-180}}°).

steps.prompt: For a gain match to $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°, the input network must present $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ (in a 50 Ω system).

ask.prompt: Find the reactance part of $Z_S$ (with sign).
ask.explanation: $X_S = 50\cdot 2|\Gamma|\sin\angle\Gamma/|1-\Gamma|^2$ = 100 × {{m11}} × sin({{-a11}}°)/{{q}} = **{{100*m11*sin(ph)/q|Ω}}**: the source must look inductive to cancel the capacitive transistor input.

steps.prompt: For a unilateral transistor, conjugately matching the input and the output separately gives the maximum transducer gain.
steps.explanation: True. With $S_{12} = 0$ the gain factors into $G_SG_0G_L$, and $G_S$ and $G_L$ are maximized independently by $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$ and $\Gamma_L = S_{22}^*$. With $S_{12} \neq 0$ the two matches interact and must be solved simultaneously.

steps.prompt: A FET has $F_{min}$ = {{Fm}} dB, $R_N$ = {{RN}} Ω, $\Gamma_{opt}$ = {{mo}}∠{{ao}}° and $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}° (unilateral). The input is matched for maximum **gain**, $\Gamma_S = S_{11}^*$. Find the resulting noise figure in dB.
An LNA uses a unilateral FET with $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°; its lossless input network presents $\Gamma_S = \Gamma_{opt}$ = {{mo}}∠{{ao}}° for minimum noise. What VSWR does the 50 Ω source see?
steps.explanation: The mismatch between $\Gamma_S$ and $\Gamma_{in} = S_{11}$ appears at the 50 Ω side as $|\Gamma_a| = \left|\frac{\Gamma_S - S_{11}^*}{1 - \Gamma_SS_{11}}\right|$. Numerator: {{nr}} + j({{ni}}); denominator: {{dr}} + j({{di}}). $|\Gamma_a|$ = {{Ga}}, VSWR = (1 + {{Ga}})/(1 − {{Ga}}) = **{{(1+Ga)/(1-Ga)}}**. This is why LNAs often have a poor input match.

steps.prompt: A transistor has $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°, $S_{21}$ = {{m21}}∠{{a21}}°, $S_{12}$ = {{m12}}∠{{a12}}°, $S_{22}$ = {{m22}}∠{{a22}}°. Check its stability and find the maximum gain with a simultaneous conjugate match, in dB.

A unilateral design uses a transistor with $S_{11}$ = {{m11}}∠{{a11}}°, $|S_{21}|$ = {{m21}}, $S_{22}$ = {{m22}}∠{{a22}}°. The matching networks present $\Gamma_S$ = {{mS}}∠{{aS}}° (a compromise for low noise) and $\Gamma_L$ = {{mL}}∠{{aL}}°. Find the transducer gain in dB.
The input of a low-noise amplifier is normally conjugately matched to the transistor, $\Gamma_S = \Gamma_{in}^*$, for maximum gain.
steps.explanation: False. For lowest noise the source must present $\Gamma_{opt}$, which usually differs from $\Gamma_{in}^*$. The LNA accepts some lost gain and a worse input match to reach a noise figure near $F_{min}$. Gain is cheap (add a stage); noise added at the input cannot be removed.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of a single-stage transistor amplifier design in order.
items: Choose the transistor and bias, and get its S-parameters (and noise parameters)
Check stability (K and |Δ|, or μ) over the whole band
Choose $\Gamma_S$ and $\Gamma_L$ for gain, noise or a compromise
Design the input and output matching networks
Simulate or measure gain, noise figure, match and stability
steps.explanation: S-parameters depend on the bias, so that comes first. A potentially unstable device restricts which terminations are allowed, so check before choosing $\Gamma_S$ and $\Gamma_L$. Then realize them with matching networks (L-sections, stubs) and verify, including out-of-band stability.
